title: Cap. VII open: De Reprobatione — prolegomena; two rocks to avoid
latin: De Reprobatione quaedam prolegomena una cum sententia Arminiana. Hisce praelibatis, alteram susceptae disputationis partem mox aggrediar, quae est de praeteritione, non-electione sive Reprobatione illarum personarum quas Deus eximia illa et speciali misericordia, quae ad vitam infallibiliter perducit, non est dignatus. Atque hic, et uspiam, obtinere debet illud Paulinum, Rom. xii. 3. μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν. Nam otiosae curiositati tantum deerits discere, quantum libuerit inquirere, ut prudenter Tertullianus, De anima, in fine. In hac ergo materia tractanda duo scopuli sunt omni cautione fugiendi.
pass_a: Certain prolegomena concerning Reprobation together with the Arminian opinion. These things having been tasted beforehand, I shall presently approach the other part of the undertaken disputation, which is concerning passing by, non-election or Reprobation of those persons whom God has not dignified with that excellent and special mercy which infallibly leads to life. And here, and everywhere, that Pauline saying ought to obtain, Rom. 12:3: not to think more highly than one ought to think. For there will only be wanting for idle curiosity to learn as much as it shall please to inquire, as Tertullian wisely, On the Soul, at the end. In this matter therefore to be treated, there are two rocks to be fled with all caution.
pass_b: Cap. VII — some prolegomena on Reprobation, with the Arminian view. Preliminaries tasted, I turn next to the other half of the dispute: passing by, non-election, or Reprobation of those God has not dignified with that excellent special mercy that infallibly leads to life. Here and everywhere Paul's word must hold (Rom. 12:3): not to think beyond what one ought. Idle curiosity will always find as much to learn as it cares to ask (so Tertullian wisely, On the Soul, at the end). In treating this matter, two rocks must be fled with all caution.

title: Cap. VII: first rock — creating some to destroy; Prosper and Hos. 13:9
latin: Unus, quo impingitur in Bonitatem Divinam; in quam illi peccare videntur, qui docent Deum absoluta primaria voluntate, omnem peccati considerationem antecedente, quosdam creasse ut perderet: atque ex hac perdendi voluntate putant dimanare quicquid circa non-electos a Deo agitur. Nos cum Prospero potius dicendum arbitramur, Aliam esse nascendi, aliam pereundi causam: Ut nascantur homines, Conditoris esse beneficium; ut pereant, praevaricatoris esse meritum. Creantur quidem a Deo, quos praevidit aeternae vitae participes nunquam fore; creantur, quos decrevit suo libero arbitrio, idque speciali gratia minime fulto, uti; creantur denique, quos decrevit propter peccata justissime damnationi subjicere. Perditio interim haec sive damnatio non finis creationis, sed merces transgressionis aestimanda est — ut semper stet illud Dei apud Hoseam, Perditio tua ex te, Hos. xiii. 9.
pass_a: One, by which one strikes upon the Divine Goodness; against which those seem to sin, who teach that God by absolute primary will, preceding every consideration of sin, created certain ones that he might destroy them: and from this will of destroying they think there flows whatever is done by God concerning the non-elect. We rather judge with Prosper that it is to be said, There is one cause of being born, another of perishing: That men are born is the Creator's benefit; that they perish is the transgressor's desert. They are indeed created by God, whom he foresaw would never be partakers of eternal life; they are created, whom he decreed to use their free choice, and that by no means propped by special grace; they are created finally, whom he decreed most justly to subject to damnation on account of sins. Meantime this perdition or damnation is to be estimated not as the end of creation, but as the wage of transgression — that that of God in Hosea may always stand, Thy destruction is from thee, Hos. 13:9.
pass_b: First rock: striking divine Goodness — those who teach God by absolute primary will, before any regard to sin, created some in order to destroy them, and that from that destroying will flows whatever God does about the non-elect. With Prosper we rather say: one cause of being born, another of perishing — birth is the Creator's benefit; perishing is the transgressor's desert. God does create those he foresaw would never share eternal life; those he decreed to use free choice with no special grace undergirding it; those he decreed most justly to subject to damnation for sins. Yet that perdition or damnation is not creation's end but transgression's wage — so Hosea may always stand: Your destruction is from you (Hos. 13:9).

lemmas.lemma: Aliam esse nascendi, aliam pereundi causam

title: Cap. VII: reprobation decree not thrust into all acts — common love; Rom. 2:4-5
latin: Porro, altum illud et arcanum non-electionis sive reprobationis decretum non est ita omnibus Dei actionibus importune ingerendum, quasi cum non-electis Deus nihil ageret, nisi ex hoc non-electionis decreto. Utcunque enim Deus quorundam noluerit eousque misereri, ut decernet eos ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter perducere, atque voluerit cosdem interveniente illorum peccato exitio destinare, tamen dum agunt in terris, atque praesertim intra Ecclesiae septa, in conferendis tum beneficiis corporalibus tum spiritualibus, atque ad salutem ex rei natura tendentibus, multa cum illis agit ex amore communi sive φιλανθρωπίᾳ, qua universum genus humanum prosequitur, multa ex foedere, quo secundum suam ordinationem omnibus Ecclesiae visibilis membris supernaturalia quaedam beneficia largitur. In eventu haec omnia Dei dona fiunt reprobis noxia et perniciosa: non tamen dicendum aut sentiendum est, Deum propter decretum reprobationis intendere abusum donorum suorum, et hostili animo ea suppeditare non-electis, ut eos hisce abutentes puniat ac perdat. Pauli potius sententia amplectanda est, qui ostendit Deum cum non-electis multa agere ex illa redundanti benignitate quae ad omnes homines se diffundit, quamvis non pari gradu aut mensura. Huc spectant illa, Rom. ii. 4. 5: An divitias bonitatis ejus et patientiae contemnis, ignorans te benignitate Dei ad resipiscentiam deduci? Sed pro duritia tua, et corde quod resipiscere nescit, thesaurizas tibi iram, etc.
pass_a: Further, that deep and secret decree of non-election or reprobation is not so awkwardly to be thrust into all God's actions, as if with the non-elect God did nothing, except from this decree of non-election. For although God was unwilling to pity certain ones so far as to decree to lead them infallibly to eternal life, and willed to destine the same to ruin with their sin intervening, yet while they act on earth, and especially within the pale of the Church, in conferring both bodily and spiritual benefits, and such as by the nature of the thing tend to salvation, he does many things with them from common love or φιλανθρωπία, with which he pursues the whole human race, many things from the covenant by which according to his ordination he bestows certain supernatural benefits on all members of the visible Church. In the event all these gifts of God become noxious and pernicious to the reprobate: yet it is not to be said or felt that God on account of the decree of reprobation intends the abuse of his gifts, and with hostile mind supplies them to the non-elect, that abusing these he may punish and destroy them. Rather Paul's sentence is to be embraced, who shows that God does many things with the non-elect from that overflowing benignity which diffuses itself to all men, though not in equal degree or measure. Hither look those things, Rom. 2:4-5: Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and patience, not knowing that thou art led by the benignity of God unto repentance? But according to thy hardness, and heart that knows not to repent, thou treasurest up wrath for thyself, etc.
pass_b: Further: that deep secret decree of non-election or reprobation must not be awkwardly stuffed into every act of God, as if with the non-elect he did nothing except from that decree. Though he would not pity some so far as to decree their infallible leading to eternal life, and willed to destine them to ruin with their sin intervening, yet while they live on earth — especially within the Church's pale — in giving bodily and spiritual benefits that by nature tend to salvation, he does much with them from common love or φιλανθρωπία toward the whole human race, and much from the covenant by which he lavishes certain supernatural benefits on all members of the visible Church. In the event those gifts become noxious to the reprobate — yet one must not say God by the reprobation decree intends abuse of his gifts, and hostilely supplies them to the non-elect so that abusing them they may be punished and destroyed. Rather take Paul's word: God does much with the non-elect from that overflowing kindness that spreads to all, though not in equal measure (Rom. 2:4-5 — or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience, not knowing God's kindness leads you to repentance? But by your hardness you treasure up wrath).

lemmas.gloss: common love toward the human race

title: Cap. VII: opposite rock — defending goodness so special mercy in election is crushed
latin: Jam vero ex adverso nonnulli sunt qui praedictum scopulum satis solicite vitant, sed interim in alium haud minus perniciosum incurrunt. Hi in decreto Reprobationis explicando bonitatem Dei ita defendunt, ut in opposito Electionis decreto specialem et ex gratuito beneplacito dimanantem misericordiam plane obruant. Quali illud Paulinum, Rom. ix. 18. Miserebor cui voluero, ac si sonaret, Miserebor ejus quem justum esse cognovero, cujus promptam fidem videro, quem praeceptis meis obedire perspexero, uti haec verba exposuit, vel potius corrupit Faustus Semipelagianus, De libero arbitrio lib. 1. cap. 3. Quod itaque de Iove suo cecinit poeta, Rex Jupiter omnibus idem, id illi de vero Deo affirmant, Illum scilicet ex aequo omnibus vitam aeternam velle, administratis autem mediis ad eam rem sufficientibus, quosdam ad gloriam eligere, dum praevidet eos hisce mediis recte usuros; alios praeterire, quia praevidet iisdem male usuros. Unde nulla in eligendo specialis Dei misericordia ostenditur, nec in reprobando Divinae voluntatis libertas ostenditur; nec denique in comparata illa consideratione, cur hic electus, iste praeteritus, ulla altitudo invenitur; sed eorum discrimen electorum et non-electorum ad libertatem humanarum voluntatum revocatur. Recte hoc fatetur Spalatensis, eos qui praedestinationem et reprobationem ex praescientia tenent debere efficaciam gratiae ponere in voluntate hominis, et media ad salutem humanam necessaria tanquam a Deo praeparata omnibus admittere, non tamen ut praedestinata ulli; De Republ. Eccl. lib. 7. cap. 11. num. 198.
pass_a: Now on the contrary there are some who avoid the aforesaid rock carefully enough, but meantime run upon another no less pernicious. These in explaining the decree of Reprobation so defend the goodness of God, that in the opposite decree of Election they plainly overwhelm the special mercy flowing from gratuitous good pleasure. As if that Pauline saying, Rom. 9:18, I will have mercy on whom I will, sounded, I will have mercy on him whom I shall know to be just, whose ready faith I shall see, whom I shall have perceived to obey my precepts — as Faustus the Semi-Pelagian exposed, or rather corrupted, these words, On Free Choice book 1 chapter 3. What therefore the poet sang of his Jupiter, King Jupiter the same to all, that they affirm of the true God, namely that he wills eternal life equally to all, and the means sufficient for that end being administered, elects certain ones to glory while he foresees they will use these means rightly; passes by others, because he foresees they will use the same ill. Whence in electing no special mercy of God is shown, nor in reprobating is the liberty of the Divine will shown; nor finally in that compared consideration, why this one elect, that one passed by, is any height found; but their discrimination of elect and non-elect is recalled to the liberty of human wills. Rightly Spalato confesses this, that those who hold predestination and reprobation from foresight ought to set the efficacy of grace in the will of man, and admit the means necessary to human salvation as prepared by God for all, yet not as predestinated to any; On the Ecclesiastical Republic book 7 chapter 11 number 198.
pass_b: Opposite rock: some carefully dodge the first, then hit another no less deadly. Explaining the reprobation decree, they so defend God's goodness that in the opposite election decree they crush special mercy flowing from gratuitous good pleasure. As if Rom. 9:18 — I will have mercy on whom I will — meant I will have mercy on him I know just, whose ready faith I see, whom I see obey my precepts (so Faustus the Semi-Pelagian exposits, or rather corrupts, On Free Choice 1.3). What the poet sang of Jupiter — King Jupiter the same to all — they affirm of the true God: he wills eternal life equally to all; with sufficient means administered, he elects to glory those he foresees will use them well, and passes by those he foresees will abuse them. So electing shows no special mercy, reprobating no liberty of divine will, and in why this one is elect and that passed by no height remains — the split is recalled to human wills' liberty. Spalato rightly grants that holders of predestination and reprobation from foresight must put grace's efficacy in man's will, and admit means to salvation as prepared by God for all, yet not as predestined to any (Ecclesiastical Republic 7.11.198).

lemmas.gloss: foresight view puts efficacy in man's will

title: Cap. VII: our sense — negative reprobation from freest will; Episcopius on not-willing the highest good
latin: Nos autem, sicuti ipsum electionis beneficium ex gratuito Dei beneplacito, non ex praeeunte aliquo hominis bono actu pendere docuimus, ita negationem ejusdem beneficii, quam non-electionem, praeteritionem, sive reprobationem negativam appellare solemus, ex eadem liberrima Dei voluntate arcessimus, facientis de suo quod vult. Qui in multis pessime, in hoc non male philosophatur Episcopius, in Thesibus suis Disput. 22. de Justific. thes. 3: Aliud longe est, inquit, non velle punire; aliud, summo bono aliquem afficere velle. Nos a pari etiam dicimus: Aliud longe est velle aliquem punire, aliud non velle aliquem summo bono afficere.
pass_a: But we, as we have taught that the benefit of election itself hangs from the gratuitous good pleasure of God, not from some preceding good act of man, so the negation of the same benefit, which we are wont to call non-election, passing by, or negative reprobation, we fetch from the same freest will of God, doing with his own what he wills. Who in many things philosophizes worst, in this not badly, Episcopius, in his Theses, Disputation 22 on Justification, thesis 3: It is one thing far, he says, not to will to punish; another, to will to affect someone with the highest good. We also say by parity: It is one thing far to will to punish someone, another not to will to affect someone with the highest good.
pass_b: But as we taught that election's benefit hangs on God's gratuitous good pleasure, not on some prior good act of man, so the negation of that benefit — which we call non-election, passing by, or negative reprobation — we fetch from the same freest will of God, doing with his own what he wills. Episcopius, often worst in philosophy, here not badly (Theses, Disp. 22 on Justification, th. 3): it is one thing not to will to punish; another to will to affect someone with the highest good. By parity we say: it is one thing to will to punish someone; another not to will to affect someone with the highest good.

lemmas.gloss: not-willing to punish vs not-willing the highest good

title: Cap. VII close (open): punishment presupposes fault; negative reprobation denies unowed benefit
latin: Prior illa voluntas puniendi in Deo considerari non potest aut debet, nisi cum respectu antecedaneo ad peccatum personae puniendae, tanquam causam demeritoriam; sed haec voluntas praetereundi, vel noluntas, ut ita loquar, praedestinandi, considerari potest absque respectu antecedaneo ad peccatum personae non-electae. Ratio autem hujus discriminis inde petenda est, quod punitio sit actus vindicativae justitiae, ac proinde culpam vindicta dignam praesupponit: Non-electio autem sive reprobatio negativa non poena sit, sed gratuiti beneficii negatio, quod Deus nemini tenetur exhibere; ac proinde ex natura rei culpam antecedaneam haud praerequirat.
pass_a: That former will of punishing in God cannot or ought not to be considered, except with antecedent respect to the sin of the person to be punished, as a demeritorious cause; but this will of passing by, or nolition, so to speak, of predestinating, can be considered without antecedent respect to the sin of the non-elect person. But the reason of this discrimination is to be sought from this, that punishment is an act of vindicative justice, and therefore presupposes a fault worthy of vengeance: But non-election or negative reprobation is not a punishment, but the negation of a gratuitous benefit, which God is bound to exhibit to no one; and therefore by the nature of the thing it hardly presupposes an antecedent fault.
pass_b: The will to punish in God cannot be considered without prior regard to the sin of the one to be punished, as demeritorious cause. But the will to pass by — or nolition, so to speak, of predestinating — can be considered without prior regard to the non-elect person's sin. Why the difference? Punishment is an act of vindicative justice, and so presupposes a fault worthy of vengeance. Non-election or negative reprobation is not a punishment, but denial of a gratuitous benefit God owes no one — and so by its nature hardly requires an antecedent fault.
